I think this problem can be extended to many devices that are not explicitly drives.  Many PCIe cards can support an independent power-off from the host.  We've seen it especially with NICs.  I'd really prefer if we can generalize this to a "sub-device power cycle".

Thank you for this feedback. Updated: the design is now "Sub-Device State Management" with a shared common layer and per-type binaries following the dbus-sensors pattern. NIC, PCIe card, or any other sub-device type is additive: new PDI interface, new binary on top of the shared layer, no changes to existing types. Drive is the first consumer.

How do you handle the relationship between the overall system and the sub-device (ie. drive)?  When the host is _off_ you also want the state of the drive to be represented as _off_.  When the host is _off_, you probably want the drive to give an error if someone asks for it to be _on_.  I don't see any words to talk about this relationship.

Thank you for the feedback. Updated the design to address this: a new "Host dependency" section under Device Type: Drive describes two layers. Systemd target wiring for execution ordering (obmc-host-stop triggers obmc-drive-poweroff), and semantic validation using the existing `Inventory.Decorator.ManagedHost` interface. When the associated host is off, On/Reboot/Powercycle transitions are rejected with a D-Bus error.
How will bmcweb know the relationship between Inventory, exposed by entity-manager, and State, exposed by your proposed daemon?

Thank you for raising this. The updated design documents this in "Inventory-to-State Mapping": the state object publishes an Association.Definitions tuple ("inventory", "state", <inventory path>), and bmcweb follows the /state association endpoint from the inventory object.

This is a new proposed pattern. A bmcweb change would be needed to follow the association. The association pattern itself is consistent with existing bmcweb association usage such as chassis-to-drive lookups.
You team definitely implemented NICs before. ;)

Fair point, thank you. NIC is now explicitly called out as a future device type. The per-type binary structure means adding NIC support requires only a new PDI interface, a new binary, and a new service file on the same shared infrastructure.
I would suggest you specify `platform-init` as potentialy impacted as it should be where we write any platform-specific initialization implementation.

Thank you. Added to Impacts: platform-init is the appropriate place for platform-specific early-boot hardware initialization (e.g. GPIO direction setup for drive power enables). The daemon has no knowledge of hardware protocols.

I don't see `openbmc/openbmc` listed here and there is a huge gap in your design: how do you specify which drives are managed by this proposal.

phosphor-state-manager was written before entity-manager so it isn't unexpected that the integration between the two is very weak; effectively non-existent for "how many chassis and hosts" do we have.  PSM hard-coded this into openbmc recipe files per-platform.

When we start to move into sub-devices, I think integration with EM becomes far more important:
- How do you express the relationship between a host and a sub-device?
- How do you express the relationship between a sub-device inventory (FRU) and state management?
- How do you handle dynamic detection of devices and/or configurations where some devices are not present?  Drives, for example, can have N NVMe slots with only M of them populated.  We shouldn't show Redfish content for power control of empty slots.

Thank you for the detailed questions. All addressed in the updated design under "Entity-Manager Integration":

Host-to-device relationship: through the existing `Inventory.Decorator.ManagedHost` interface. The design's config example shows ManagedHost with HostIndex on the drive Board entity.

Inventory-to-state relationship: through a D-Bus association ("inventory", "state", <inventory path>) published by the state object. This would require a bmcweb change to follow the association endpoint instead of the current same-path lookup.

Dynamic detection: the daemon watches entity-manager InterfacesAdded/InterfacesRemoved. Platforms can use gpio-presence with DevicePresence Probe for SSD slots. When a device is absent, gpio-presence removes the DevicePresence interface, entity-manager tears down the Board entity, and the state daemon destroys the state object. No inventory means no Redfish resource.

Detection is independent of FRU availability: drives without FRU EEPROM use GPIO presence detection, drives with FRU use FruDevice Probe, and the daemon is agnostic to the detection mechanism.

If you use function pointer / per-platform lookup tables then it is already decoupled.


The problem with decoupling it with systemd targets is that it prevents people from refactoring this design or implementation in the future.

Since you provide extension points via systemd which can then be used by downstream code or platform maintainers.

> Just to confirm my understanding: with a function-pointer / lookup-table
 approach, would platform-specific hardware operations (GPIO, I2C, etc.)
 need to be compiled into the state manager binary, or would some other 
mechanism be used to keep them separate?

It would be my preference for things to be compiled into the state manager to reduce the runtime overhead of starting whole new processes for simple operations like i2c transfers or gpio changes. That's a few function calls in C++ with minimal overhead.

If you want to have a clean separation then each platform could get it's own sub-directory similarly to how this is already done in `platform-init` repository.

The platform could then implement various function calls from an abstract base class which the common code in the device state manager then calls into depending on for which platform it was compiled for or which one was detected at runtime.

The benefit of this approach is that the platform logic is done in C++, goes through full static analysis, and the maintainer will have full overview into it and is able to refactor things in the future.

A similar design was implemented for `phosphor-bmc-code-mgmt` where common code calls into device specific update code. In that repo there are still multiple binaries and multiple processes though.

Thank you for the detailed suggestion and the `phosphor-bmc-code-mgmt` reference.
I've incorporated the compiled-in approach as a documented alternative in the latest patchset's Alternatives Considered section, including the per-platform sub-directory pattern and the static analysis benefits you described.

The design currently uses systemd targets to match the existing host/chassis pattern, but this is an open design point. Once Patrick and Andrew decide on the preferred direction, I'll update accordingly.

Thanks, since you outlined the benefits of the compiled-in approach, this one is resolved from my side. If they still want to go with a decoupled design based on the tradeoffs then it's for them to decide i guess.

Why a new binary? Can't the various types not share one binary and then select via `argv[1]` which code path is run?

I would expect the total compressed size of the binaries to be less if it was combined into one binary or even combined with existing state manager binary.

Merging things like that already resulted in compressed size reduction of the bmcweb.
Resolving this since the alternative and tradeoff is now written down. Let's see what maintainers decide.

It can never appear like this. The `Item.Drive` has lots of properties which need to exist when the interface is created.

https://github.com/openbmc/phosphor-dbus-interfaces/blob/master/yaml/xyz/openbmc_project/Inventory/Item/Drive.interface.yaml
You're right. I will update it to include all `Item.Drive` properties with their PDI default values.
Done

So platforms need to do their own service wiring to get a sane default behavior?

This reminds me of the `rsyslog` story where each platform was copy-pasting the same configuration to get Redfish EventLog to work.


Is it possible to instead inline that behavior into the code directly or configure it via EM?


Why do we need this infinite flexibility on the platform side to start whichever services when it's only 2 cases here. Either the drives power off with the host, or they do not. Is there other cases?

Thank you for the concrete example with rsyslog.

I think for the common case (drives power off with host), the daemon could handle this internally: observe CurrentHostState for the associated host and initiate poweroff for drives with matching `ManagedHost` when the host goes off. That way platforms would not need any systemd wiring for host-drive power dependency.

Platform-specific target hooks would still be needed for the actual hardware power control (GPIO, I2C), since that varies per platform.

I will update the doc to propose this approach and clarify the distinction.
Alright, it is good to at least have the default case be a builtin. Thanks for explaining it to me 👍
Updated in the latest patchset.

IMO process crash is not in scope for consideration. Why would we design for our code to crash? If there is a bug we can fix it?

And what do you mean with 'upgrade'?

Do you mean updating individual packages on the BMC and restarting them individually?
Agreed, crash isolation is a secondary consideration. The wording in Alternatives could be clearer on that. I will revise it.
Acknowledged

> and the binary always links
  every supported type with no per-platform selection.

You can always configure the supported features with meson options.
Agreed, meson options can achieve per-platform type selection as well.
Acknowledged

The host power state tracking is also replicated. The linux per process overhead is also replicated. The overall binary size increases since `-Osize` does not work properly  due to duplicated codes.

The overhead of system services and associated metadata tracking is also duplicated. There is also additional logs generated from service startup.


One of my use-cases is to be able to emulate things in qemu.

While per-instance and per-type designs may run okay on a real hardware, they are significantly less efficient than single-binary single-process designs.

Since lots of developers rely on qemu, i would be happy if we could prioritize optimal solutions in regards to memory use, binary size and runtime overhead.

Thank you for the detailed review and feedback.

The sub-device daemons are expected to be much smaller than bmcweb, and each new device type would add incrementally (the shared infrastructure is built once, per-type code is minimal). That said, I understand the efficiency argument for a consolidated approach, and a single binary with type selection is feasible.

My starting point was the existing per-type binary convention in PSM and dbus-sensors, with the practical benefit of recipe-level inclusion/exclusion. But I am open to either direction.

@patrick@stwcx.xyz @geissonator@yahoo.com do you have a preference between per-type binaries vs a single combined sub-device
binary? Happy to implement whichever you prefer.
Thanks for adding all these considerations to 'Alternatives considered'.

Hi @patrick@stwcx.xyz @geissonator@yahoo.com,

I've significantly reworked the design based on earlier feedback, switching to an entity-manager-driven discovery approach.

Could you please take a look when you get a chance? I'm happy to make further adjustments based on your feedback.

Thanks.
